newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco deal could have little affect on US ouput.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco deal could have little affect on US ouput.

text.p: U.S. tobacco production could be relatively unaffected by a landmark agreement reached last week between state attorneys general and the U.S. tobacco industry, a U.S. agriculture department economist said Monday.

"There's not going to be a real immediate affect," Tom Capehart, a tobacco analyst in USDA's Economic Research Service, told Reuters. Any drop in consumption might affect imports more than domestic output, he said.

Despite its high profile, tobacco is a relatively minor U.S. crop. USDA has pegged U.S. plantings this year at 807,000 acres, up 10 percent from last year, but still tiny in comparison to an estimated 81.4 million acres of corn plantings.

The agreement, which still must be approved by Congress, calls for the tobacco companies to make payments totalling $365.8-billion over the next 25 years. The annual industry payments would also be adjusted for inflation by 3 percent each year.

"It's a huge settlement," which at first glance seems to likely to push up cigarette prices, Capehart said. But "their advertising expenditures are going to plummett," which could offset a substantial portion of the settlement, he said.
According to the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, the tobacco industry spent $4.83 billion on advertising and other promotional expenses in 1994, down from $6.03 billion in 1993.

Over 25 years, that would equal about $120 to $150 billion, unadjusted for inflation. The settlement would sharply cut those expenditures by banning advertising on billboards and outdoor signs and many other activities, Capehart said.

If tobacco companies do boost prices, that would further reduce U.S. demand, he said. But to "maintain their political base," the tobacco industry would likely cut imports before reducing domestic purchases, Capehart said.

Meanwhile, the settlement may increase the chance that Congress will eliminate the tobacco program, which supports tobacco grower income by limiting the amount of tobacco that can be grown each year, he said.
If that happens, higher prices for tobacco compared to other crops could encourage more plantings and lead to an increase in U.S. tobacco production, he said.
Depending on relative prices, those additional tobacco acres could come from cotton, soybeans or other southern crops, Capehart said.
